Many tailors in Nigeria learned in apprenticeship by **cutting directly on the fabric** with chalk, using the client's measurements and years of practice. It works, and some masters are very good at it. But it has limits: every garment starts from zero, a cutting mistake ruins expensive fabric, and it is hard to make ten identical dresses or to teach an apprentice exactly what you did. **Pattern making** solves these problems by putting the shape on paper first.
A set square ruler used for drawing right angles
Pattern making moves the thinking onto paper, where a mistake costs a sheet of paper, not a piece of lace.
Three kinds of pattern

A **block** (in American books called a **sloper**) is a basic, close-fitting shape with no style lines, no seam allowance and no design details. It is drafted from one person's measurements, or from a size chart, and then tested and corrected. You keep it on card and never cut fabric from it directly. The most common blocks are the **bodice block** (upper body), the **skirt block**, the **sleeve block** and the **trouser block**.

A **working pattern** is made by tracing the block and changing it to create a design: moving darts, adding a flare, lowering a neckline, cutting a princess line. A **production pattern** is the final version with seam allowances, notches, grain lines, labels and cutting instructions added, ready to lay on fabric. In a factory, the production pattern is also **graded** into a range of sizes, which you will learn in Module 3.

Why blocks pay off for a busy tailor
**Speed:** once a regular client's block fits, a new style starts from a tested shape, so you skip most fitting problems.
**Less waste:** you can lay paper pieces on the fabric and plan the cut before using scissors, which matters when a client brings exactly 6 yards of ankara or a costly lace.
**Repeatability:** for aso-ebi orders or small retail runs, every piece is cut from the same pattern, so the 20th dress matches the first.
**Teaching:** an apprentice can trace and cut from a labelled pattern long before she can cut freehand.
**Records:** a client's block, kept in a labelled envelope, is a record of her shape that you can update when her measurements change.
The garment journey

Whether you make one bespoke gown or fifty uniform shirts, the stages are the same. You agree the design, take measurements, draft or adapt the block, create the working pattern, test it in cheap fabric (a **toile**, also called a muslin), correct it, make the production pattern, cut and sew the real garment, then do a final fitting and finishing. Skipping the toile is the most common reason a beautiful fabric ends up as a garment that pulls or gapes.

Worked example: is a block worth the time?
For example, Bisi runs a small shop in Ibadan. Her regular client Funmi orders about six outfits a year, mostly fitted gowns and skirt-and-blouse sets in ankara and lace.
Without a block, Bisi spends about 2 hours per outfit adjusting fit across two or three fittings: 6 outfits × 2 hours = 12 hours a year on fit alone.
Drafting and testing a bodice and skirt block for Funmi takes about 5 hours once, including one toile.
With a tested block, Bisi estimates fit time drops to about 45 minutes per outfit: 6 × 0.75 = 4.5 hours.
Time saved in the first year: 12 − (5 + 4.5) = 2.5 hours. In the second year, with no new block needed, she saves about 12 − 4.5 = 7.5 hours.

The block pays for itself in the first year and saves more every year after, and Funmi gets better-fitting clothes with fewer fittings. Bisi decides to make blocks for her five most regular clients first.

A pattern can only be as good as the numbers it is drafted from. A 2 cm error in the bust becomes a dress that is too tight to zip or loose enough to gape. Most measuring errors come from three habits: pulling the tape too tight, letting it slope at the back, and measuring over thick clothing. Fix those three and your accuracy improves straight away.
A straight ruler for measuring
Accurate numbers are the foundation of every block you will draft.
Prepare before you measure
Use a good tape measure that has not stretched. Check it against a metal ruler: 30 cm on the tape should be exactly 30 cm.
Ask the client to wear a thin, well-fitting top or the bra she will wear under the garment. A padded or minimiser bra changes the bust by several centimetres.
Tie a narrow tape, ribbon or elastic snugly around the **natural waist** (the narrowest part of the torso, where the body bends sideways). Every length is taken to this line.
Ask her to stand naturally, feet together, arms relaxed, looking straight ahead. People often hold their breath or stand very straight when measured, which gives false numbers.

Cross-check your numbers

Before the client leaves, check the card for numbers that do not make sense. Measuring twice and comparing is the simplest check: if two readings differ by more than 1 cm, measure a third time. Then look at relationships. Front shoulder to waist is normally longer than nape to waist on a woman with a full bust, because the tape travels over the bust. Hip is usually larger than bust for a pear shape and smaller for an apple shape, but a hip much smaller than the waist suggests a mistake. Across back and across front should each be roughly similar to each other, within a few centimetres.

Worked example: catching a measuring error
For example, Chiamaka is measuring a new client, Ruth, in Enugu for a fitted ankara gown.
First readings: bust 98 cm, waist 82 cm, hip 104 cm, nape to waist 39 cm, front shoulder to waist 37 cm.
She notices the front length (37 cm) is shorter than the back length (39 cm), which is unusual for a woman with a 98 cm bust.
She re-measures the front and finds she had gone around, not over, the bust point. The correct front shoulder to waist is 43 cm.
She re-checks the back length and sees the waist tape had slipped down at the back. The correct nape to waist is 38 cm.
Final card: bust 98, waist 82, hip 104, nape to waist 38, front shoulder to waist 43.
A 6 cm error in front length would have made the bodice ride up and the waist seam sit above Ruth's waist. Two quick cross-checks saved a refitting and possibly a whole bodice.
The measurement card

Keep one card or notebook page per client, with her first name, phone number, the date, the unit (cm), every measurement, and notes on posture such as "right shoulder slightly lower" or "prefers loose waist". Many tailors also keep a copy in a phone note or spreadsheet. Measurements change over time, after pregnancy or with weight change, so re-measure a regular client at least once a year and before any special-occasion outfit.
Respect and privacy

Measuring is personal. Explain what you will measure before you start, measure in a private space, and allow the client to bring a friend if she prefers. Body measurements are private information: do not post or share a client's card or numbers in WhatsApp groups, even for aso-ebi coordination, without her permission.

If you draft a pattern exactly to the body measurements, the garment will be skin tight. The client could not breathe, sit or lift her arms. The extra room added on purpose is called **ease**. Understanding ease is what separates a pattern maker from someone copying numbers.
A pair of black-handled scissors
Good tools and correct allowances matter as much as good measurements.
Two kinds of ease

**Wearing ease** is the minimum room needed to move comfortably. It is built into the block. **Design ease** is extra room added for style: a loose boubou or kaftan has a lot of design ease; a fitted mermaid gown has almost none beyond wearing ease. Stretch fabrics are different again: knit garments are often drafted with zero or even negative ease, meaning the pattern is smaller than the body and the fabric stretches to fit.

These are common starting points, not fixed laws. Different drafting systems use different amounts, and the right ease also depends on the fabric: stiff brocade or aso-oke feels tighter than soft cotton at the same measurement. You confirm ease in the toile. Because most blocks are drafted as a quarter of the body (half the front and half the back), you divide total ease by four. For 6 cm bust ease, each quarter gets 1.5 cm.

Worked example: from body to pattern width
For example, Ada is drafting a fitted ankara dress for a client with a 96 cm bust. She wants 6 cm of bust ease and will use 1.5 cm seam allowances at the side seams.
Body quarter: 96 ÷ 4 = 24 cm.
Ease per quarter: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cm, so the block quarter at the bust is 24 + 1.5 = 25.5 cm.
Check the full block: 25.5 × 4 = 102 cm, which is the body (96) plus ease (6).
On the production pattern, she adds 1.5 cm at the side seam of the front and back pieces. Seam allowances do not change the finished size; they are sewn away.
Ada's block measures 25.5 cm per quarter at the bust and the finished dress measures 102 cm round, giving her client 6 cm of room to breathe and move.

A safe work space
Common workshop hazards

Keep shears closed and pointing down when you carry them, and store rotary cutters with the blade guard on. Do not hold pins in your mouth, because they can be swallowed or inhaled. Switch off the sewing machine before threading it or changing the needle, and keep fingers to the side of the presser foot. Hot irons cause burns: stand the iron on its heel, unplug it when you leave the table, and keep the cord out of walkways. Do not overload one extension socket with an iron and several machines, and use a stabiliser or surge protector if your power supply fluctuates.

Look after your body too. Pattern drafting means long hours bent over a table. A table at roughly hip height, good daylight or a bright lamp, and a short stretch every hour reduce back and eye strain. Keep a small first aid box with plasters and burn gel in the shop, and teach apprentices where it is.

There are many published drafting systems, and each uses slightly different formulas. This lesson uses a widely taught **quarter method**: you draft half of the back and half of the front, each representing one quarter of the body width. Treat every formula below as a starting point. Your toile, not the formula, has the final word.
A sharpened pencil
Draft in pencil first, so lines can be corrected before you commit them in pen.
The measurement card we will use

For example, the client is Kemi: bust 96 cm, waist 78 cm, neck 36 cm, nape to waist 39 cm, front shoulder to waist 44 cm, shoulder length 12 cm, across back 35 cm, across front 33 cm, bust point height 26 cm, bust point span 18 cm. Ease: 6 cm at bust and 4 cm at waist, so 1.5 cm and 1 cm per quarter.
Drafting the back
Draw a vertical line near the left edge of the paper for the **centre back (CB)**. Mark the nape point A near the top.
From A, measure down the nape to waist length, 39 cm, and mark the waist B. Square across.
From A, measure down the armhole depth and mark C. A common starting value is bust ÷ 8 + 10 cm: 96 ÷ 8 + 10 = 22 cm. Square across from C; this is the **bust line**.
On the bust line, measure out bust ÷ 4 + ease: 24 + 1.5 = 25.5 cm. Mark D and square down to the waist line. This is the side seam guide.
Back neck: square out from A about 7 cm (a common starting value is neck ÷ 6 + 1 cm) and rise 2 cm. Draw a shallow curve from A to this neck point.

Shoulder: from the neck point, draw the shoulder line sloping down about 4 cm over its length, and make it 12.5 cm long (shoulder length plus 0.5 cm, which is eased into the front shoulder when sewing).
Across back: halfway between A and C, measure out half the across back plus 0.5 cm: 17.5 + 0.5 = 18 cm. Draw the armhole curve from the shoulder point, through this mark, down to D.

Waist: the waist quarter is waist ÷ 4 + ease: 19.5 + 1 = 20.5 cm. The bust line is 25.5 cm, so 5 cm must be removed. Take 2 cm at the side seam and put 3 cm into a back waist dart about 9 cm from CB, its point 2 cm below the bust line.
Drafting the front
Draw a vertical **centre front (CF)** line. The front is drafted with the same bust line width (25.5 cm) and the same waist quarter (20.5 cm).
Front neck: neck width about the same as the back (7 cm), and neck depth about 1 cm more than the width, so 8 cm down CF. Draw a smooth curve.
Shoulder: slope the front shoulder about 5 cm and make it 12 cm long.
Bust point: measure 26 cm from the neck point down towards the bust line, and 9 cm (half the bust span) in from CF. Mark the bust point clearly.
Front length: measure 44 cm from the neck point over the bust point to the waist. This sets the front waist, which sits lower than the back because of the bust.
Across front: half of 33 plus 0.5 = 17 cm, placed about 5 cm above the bust line. Draw the armhole curve.
Front waist dart: 5 cm must be removed at the waist; take 2 cm at the side seam and 3 cm in a dart under the bust point, ending 2 to 3 cm below it.
Worked example: finding the side bust dart
For example, after drafting, Kemi's tailor measures both side seams from the underarm (bust line at the side) down to the waist.
Back side seam: 17 cm (39 cm nape to waist minus 22 cm armhole depth).
Front side seam: 20.5 cm, longer because the front waist was dropped for the bust.
Difference: 20.5 − 17 = 3.5 cm. The side seams must be the same length to sew together, so the front needs a 3.5 cm side bust dart.
She draws the dart from the front side seam about 5 cm below the underarm, with legs 3.5 cm apart at the side seam, pointing to the bust point and stopping 2.5 cm short of it.
She folds the dart closed and checks that the front side seam now measures 17 cm, matching the back.
The 3.5 cm side dart takes in exactly the extra front length created by the bust, so the side seams match and the bodice shapes over the bust without pulling.

Dart manipulation: moving darts and creating style lines
Explain why darts can be moved anywhere around the bust point without changing fit
Move a dart using the pivot method and the slash-and-spread method
Turn darts into a princess seam, gathers or tucks
Shape and true a dart so the seam line stays smooth

A dart is a wedge of fabric folded and stitched away to turn flat cloth into a three-dimensional shape. On the front bodice, every dart points at the **bust point**. That is the key idea of dart manipulation: as long as the dart still points to the bust point and removes the same amount of shape, you can move it anywhere around the edge of the pattern. Shoulder, neckline, armhole, side seam, waist or centre front: the fit stays the same, only the look changes.
A simple dress
Most bodice styles, from a classic darted top to a corset-look gown, start as the same block with darts moved.
Method 1: pivot
Trace the front block onto new paper. Mark the bust point and the existing dart (for example the side dart).
Mark where you want the new dart, for example the middle of the shoulder. Draw a line from there to the bust point.
Put a pin or pencil point on the bust point. Trace the pattern from the new dart position, round the neck and CF, down to the first leg of the old dart.
Pivot the block on the bust point until the old dart is closed (the two legs meet). Trace the rest of the outline, round the side and back up to the new dart position.
The gap that opens at the shoulder is the new dart. Draw its legs to the bust point.
Method 2: slash and spread

Trace the block and cut it out. Draw a line from the new dart position to the bust point and cut along it, stopping just at the bust point so a small hinge of paper remains. Cut one leg of the old dart up to the bust point too. Fold the old dart closed and tape it. The new slash opens by itself. Tape the piece onto fresh paper and trace. Many beginners find slash and spread easier to understand because they can see the shape move.

Finishing a dart properly
**Shorten from the bust point.** A dart stitched right to the bust point makes a sharp peak. End bust darts about 2 to 3 cm short of the bust point, and a little further on a fuller bust.
**Equal legs.** Both dart legs must be the same length, or the seam will not match when sewn.

**Shape the dart end.** Fold the dart closed in the direction it will be pressed (vertical darts towards the centre, horizontal darts downwards), then cut along the pattern edge. When you open it, the edge has a small point, called the dart **cap**, that makes the seam line straight after sewing.
**Mark clearly.** Notch both legs at the edge and mark the point with a small circle so it can be transferred to fabric with chalk or a tailor's tack.
Worked example: a princess-line bodice for an aso-ebi gown
For example, Halima in Kano has an aso-ebi order for a fitted lace gown with princess seams. She starts from the client's front block, which has a 3.5 cm side dart and a 3 cm waist dart.
She moves the side dart into the shoulder using the pivot method, so the front now has a shoulder dart and a waist dart, both pointing at the bust point.
She draws a smooth curved line from the shoulder dart, through the bust point, down to the waist dart. This is the princess line.
She cuts along the line to separate the centre front panel and the side front panel, and removes the dart wedges.
Where the two panels meet over the bust, she smooths the curves so there are no points, and notches both panels 5 cm above and 5 cm below the bust point so they match when sewn.
She measures the two seam edges: they should be the same length, within 0.3 cm, before seam allowance is added.
The darts have disappeared into a flattering princess seam that shapes the lace over the bust and waist. Because the shape came from the tested block, the fit is the same as the darted bodice.

Fabric, Grading and Finishing to a Professional Standard

A perfect pattern can still fail on the wrong fabric or with poor finishing. This module covers choosing and preparing Nigerian fabrics, laying out and estimating yardage, grading a pattern into a size range for aso-ebi and retail work, and finishing and inspecting garments to a standard clients pay more for.

Clients often arrive with the fabric already bought. Your job is to tell them honestly whether it suits the style, how much is needed, and how to treat it. A tailor who understands fabric avoids the classic disasters: a dress that shrinks after its first wash, a skirt that twists to one side, or a print that runs upside down on one panel.
A spool of thread
Fabric, thread and grain work together; choosing well starts before cutting.
Grain: the direction of the threads

Woven fabric has two sets of threads. The **straight grain** (warp) runs parallel to the **selvedge**, the firm finished edge. It is the strongest direction and stretches least. The **cross grain** (weft) runs from selvedge to selvedge and gives a little more. The **bias** runs at 45 degrees and stretches most, which is why bias-cut garments drape and cling. Every pattern piece carries a grain line arrow. When you lay it down, measure from each end of the arrow to the selvedge: both distances must be equal. A piece cut even slightly off grain can twist after sewing and washing.

Shrinkage test and pre-treatment

Do not guess how much a fabric will shrink. Cut a square exactly 20 cm by 20 cm, mark it with a pen, wash and dry it the way the client will wash the garment, press it, and measure again. If it now measures 19 cm along the straight grain, it shrank 5 percent that way. Wash the whole piece before cutting, or add that amount to your lengths. Also check colour bleeding by washing the square with a white cloth. Fabrics labelled dry clean only, many laces and George among them, should not be pre-washed, but you can steam press them to settle the fibres.
Iron temperature

Always test the iron on a scrap first. Cotton tolerates a hot iron, but many laces, sequinned fabrics and synthetic linings melt or pucker at high heat. Use a press cloth (a piece of plain cotton) between the iron and delicate or shiny fabrics, and never press directly on sequins or metallic threads.
Estimating yardage

One yard is 0.9144 m, so a 6-yard piece of ankara is about 5.49 m long. Widths vary, and ankara is often around 112 to 117 cm (44 to 46 inches) wide, but always measure the piece in front of you. To estimate, lay your paper pattern pieces on the floor or table within a rectangle the width of the fabric, folded in half if pieces are cut on the fold, and measure how long the layout is. Add extra for matching a large print and for shrinkage.
Worked example: will 6 yards be enough?

She lays out the pattern on a 57 cm wide folded rectangle (half the width). Bodice front and back side by side: 45 cm of length.
Skirt front and back panels are too wide to sit side by side on the fold, so they go one after the other: 2 × 125 cm = 250 cm.
Sleeves side by side: 35 cm. Facings and zip guard tucked into gaps: no extra length.

Total: 45 + 250 + 35 + 30 + 15 = 375 cm, about 3.75 m. The piece is about 5.49 m.
The gown needs about 3.75 m, leaving about 1.7 m, enough for the headwrap. Amaka tells the client before cutting, so there is no argument later about "missing" fabric.

**Grading** means making a pattern larger or smaller in a planned way, so a design keeps the same style and proportions across a range of sizes. It is not the same as photocopying a pattern bigger. If you enlarged a size 12 bodice by 10 percent all over, the neck would grow as much as the bust, and the dress would gape at the neckline. In real bodies, the bust, waist and hip change a lot between sizes, while the neck, shoulder and length change only a little.

Size charts and grade rules

A **size chart** lists the body measurements for each size. A **grade rule** tells you how much each point on the pattern moves between sizes. Published size charts differ between countries and brands, so a small Nigerian business is often better off building its own chart from the measurements of the clients it actually serves. Turning size changes into point movements

Because the block is a quarter of the body, every girth change is divided by four. A 4 cm bust change means each quarter grows 1 cm at the bust line. You can split that 1 cm: for example 0.5 cm in the side seam and 0.5 cm through the body (shared between across back and the armhole), so the shoulder and neck do not move too far. Neck width changes by about one sixth of the neck change, so a 1 cm neck change moves the neck point only about 0.2 cm. Length changes are added between the shoulder and the waist line.
Worked example: grading Kemi's bodice from L to XL
For example, Kemi's tested size L block is chosen as the base size for a group of 25 aso-ebi gowns for her cousin's wedding. Six women in the group measure close to the XL row.

Bust change L to XL: 4 cm, so each quarter grows 1 cm. On the back and front, draw a vertical cut line from the armhole, just below the across mark, straight down to the waist, and spread it 0.5 cm. Move the side seam out 0.5 cm.
Waist change: 4 cm, so the waist quarter also grows 1 cm, shared the same way: 0.5 cm through the spread and 0.5 cm at the side.
Length change: 0.5 cm. Draw a horizontal cut line between the armhole and the waist and spread it 0.5 cm, so the waist drops while the armhole stays the same shape.

Neck change: 1 cm. Move the neck point out about 0.2 cm and lower the front neck about 0.2 cm. Move the shoulder point out 0.5 cm, so the shoulder length grows 0.3 cm (0.5 minus the 0.2 neck shift), and redraw the armhole to the spread.
Check: new bust quarter = 25.5 + 1 = 26.5 cm, and 26.5 × 4 = 106 cm, which is the XL bust (100) plus 6 cm ease. Shoulder length is now about 12.3 cm.
The XL block keeps the same style and ease as the L block. Redrawing the curves smoothly between the moved points gives a pattern ready for a toile on one of the XL clients.

Aso-ebi orders bring a mix of figures, ages and preferences under one deadline. Clients judge a tailor by what they see when they turn a garment inside out and by how it looks after a few washes. Neat seams, a smooth zip, a level hem and no loose threads are what make a client pay a higher price and come back. This lesson turns quality into a routine you can check.

Press as you sew

Press every seam after you sew it and before you cross it with another seam. First press the seam flat as it was sewn to set the stitches, then press it open or to one side. Press darts over a rounded surface such as a tailor's ham or a rolled towel, so the shape stays curved: vertical darts towards the centre, horizontal darts downwards. Pressing is lifting and lowering the iron; ironing is sliding it. On fitted garments, press, do not iron, so the fabric does not stretch.
Stitch quality
A stitch length of about 2.5 mm suits most woven fabrics; use about 2 mm on curves and fine fabrics and a longer stitch for basting.
Use a new needle for each major project and match the needle to the fabric: finer for chiffon and lace, heavier for aso-oke and denim.
Backstitch or tie off at the start and end of every seam, except at dart points, where you tie the threads in a knot so the point stays flat.
Check the tension on a scrap of the same fabric: the stitches should look the same on both sides with no loops.
Measuring against the specification

A **specification** (spec) lists what the finished garment should measure at key points: bust, waist, hip, length, sleeve length. A **tolerance** is how far it may vary and still pass. For bespoke work, many tailors aim to be within about 0.5 cm at the bust and waist and about 1 cm on lengths. Set your own tolerances, write them down, and measure every garment before delivery.
Worked example: final inspection of an aso-ebi gown
For example, Grace in Port Harcourt is checking gown 14 of a 20-gown aso-ebi order before delivery. The spec for this client is: bust 104 cm, waist 86 cm, hip 110 cm, length 150 cm.
She measures the finished gown flat and doubles the half measurements: bust 104.5 cm, waist 86 cm, hip 108.5 cm, length 149.5 cm.
Against her tolerances (±0.5 cm girths, ±1 cm lengths): bust passes, waist passes, length passes, but hip is 1.5 cm small, so it fails.
She checks the side seam allowances: there is 2 cm left, so she re-sews each side seam 0.4 cm closer to the raw edge at the hip. That adds 0.8 cm per seam, 1.6 cm in total.
She re-measures: hip 110.1 cm, within tolerance. She then trims threads, checks the zip and hem, and presses.
Gown 14 passes inspection. Because Grace measures every gown, the problem was found in her shop and not at the client's fitting on the morning of the wedding.

Common last-minute faults

Uneven hem (check with the client standing, measured from the floor), wavy zip (often from stretching the fabric while sewing it), lace edges scratching the skin (fix with lining or a soft binding), and chalk or pen marks left visible (test removal on a scrap before marking).
Zips and hems

Two details decide how finished a gown looks. For an invisible zip, sew it before the side or back seam below it is closed, keep the fabric flat without stretching it, and check that waist seams and print lines meet exactly across the zip. For hems, let a bias-cut or flared skirt hang for a day before levelling, because the fabric drops. Mark the hem on the client standing in her shoes, measuring the same distance from the floor all round, then finish by hand with a blind stitch on formal wear, or by machine on everyday cotton.

Keep a simple quality log: garment number, client first name, measurements found, pass or fail, and what was fixed. Over a month, the log shows your most common faults. If hems fail often, the fix might be to mark hems on the client at the last fitting rather than in the workshop.

Pricing, Clients and Your Pattern-Making Portfolio

Skill becomes income when you price correctly, manage orders professionally and can show your work. This module covers costing a bespoke garment and an aso-ebi order, written client agreements and safe payments, photographing a portfolio, and completing your certificate project with a 90-day plan.
Costing and pricing bespoke garments and aso-ebi orders
List every cost in a garment: materials, labour, overheads and profit
Calculate an hourly labour rate and an overhead charge per garment

Many skilled tailors earn less than they should because they price by guessing or by copying the shop next door. A good price covers four things: **materials** you buy, your **labour** (and your apprentices'), **overheads** such as rent, power and data, and **profit** that lets the business grow. If any of the four is missing, you are paying for the client's outfit yourself.
A paper receipt
Every garment's price should be built from real costs, written down.
Step 1: materials

Even when the client brings the main fabric, you supply lining, interfacing, zips, thread, buttons, hooks, boning for corset bodices and sometimes stones or beads. Keep receipts and a price list in your notebook. Prices change often in Nigerian markets, so update the list every month.
Step 2: labour

Decide what your time is worth per hour. One way: choose the monthly income you need from sewing, and divide by the hours you actually sew in a month. Then time yourself on each stage of a garment (pattern, cutting, sewing, fittings, finishing). Pattern work is skilled work and belongs in the price: a new block or a complicated style takes hours.
Step 3: overheads

Add up monthly costs that are not tied to one garment: shop rent, electricity bills and generator fuel, phone data, machine servicing, needles, transport to the market. Divide by the number of garments you finish in a typical month. This gives an overhead charge per garment.

For example, Ifeoma in Lagos is pricing a fitted, lined lace gown. The client brings the lace. All naira figures are approximate and for illustration only.

If she has changed her mind about the style, or her size has changed since the fitting, explain your alteration policy calmly and give a price. Presenting your portfolio

Keep captions short and factual, for example "Toile: neckline gaped 1.5 cm. Corrected on paper. Final: no gape." A clear before-and-after story shows skill better than a large number of photos.

Measure your progress during the 90 days with a few simple numbers you can count: fittings needed per order, garments finished per week, orders delivered on the agreed date, and income after costs. Write them at the end of each month in the same notebook as your quality log. If a number is not improving, change one thing in your process and check again the next month.
Your 90-day plan
A good plan is specific and measurable. Pick one main goal for the next three months and break it into monthly targets. Keep it realistic for your time, money and family responsibilities.
**Month 1:** draft and test blocks for five regular clients; update your costing sheet with current market prices.
**Month 2:** use the blocks for at least eight orders; record fittings needed per order and compare with before.
**Month 3:** grade one tested design into three sizes and offer it to a group or as a small ready-to-wear batch; photograph and add it to your catalogue.
**Every week:** add entries to your quality log and note one improvement.

Check that every photo is clear and labelled, that numbers on your cards and costing sheets add up, and that you have the client's permission for any photo that shows her face. Then confirm the practical task is complete in the app before you take the final quiz.

Many of us learned to cut straight on the fabric with chalk. It works, but every garment starts from zero, and one cutting mistake ruins expensive fabric.
A block is a plain, close-fitting shape on paper, with no style lines and no seam allowance. Once it fits, every new style starts from a tested shape.
For example, Bisi in Ibadan worked out that a block for her regular client Funmi pays for itself in the first year, and saves about 7.5 hours a year after that.
Before you measure
Fix three habits, gain accuracy
Check your tape against a metal ruler
Thin top, and the bra she will wear
Tie a tape at the natural waist
Tape snug and level, never tight
A 2 cm error at the bust gives a dress too tight to zip. First, check your tape against a metal ruler. 30 cm on the tape must be exactly 30 cm.
Measure over a thin top and the bra she will wear, because a padded bra changes the bust by several centimetres.
Tie a narrow tape around her natural waist, the narrowest part, where the body bends sideways. Every length is taken to this line.
Keep the tape flat and level all the way round the back, with room to slide one finger under it. Do not add ease while measuring.
Worked example
Chiamaka catches a measuring error
Front length 37 cm, back length 39 cm
Front shorter than back? Unusual!
Tape went around the bust point: really 43 cm
Waist tape slipped at the back: really 38 cm
Measure twice. A gap of more than 1 cm: measure again.
For example, Chiamaka in Enugu measures a new client, Ruth, who has a 98 cm bust.
Her first readings show the front shoulder to waist as 37 cm, and the back, nape to waist, as 39 cm.
But on a woman with a full bust, the front is normally longer than the back, because the tape travels over the bust. Something is wrong.
She re-measures and finds she had gone around the bust point, not over it. The correct front length is 43 cm.
And the waist tape had slipped at the back. The correct back length is 38 cm.
A 6 cm error would have made the bodice ride up. Two quick cross-checks saved a refitting. Date every card, and re-measure regular clients at least once a year.
Ease
Room to breathe, sit and move
Wearing ease: room to move, built into the block
Design ease: extra room for style
Bust about 5 to 8 cm, waist about 2 to 4 cm
Hip about 4 to 6 cm, so she can sit
A pattern drafted exactly to the body is skin tight. The extra room you add on purpose is called ease. Wearing ease is the minimum room needed to move comfortably.
Design ease is extra room for style, plenty in a boubou, almost none in a mermaid gown.
For a fitted woven block, common starting points are about 5 to 8 cm at the bust, and about 2 to 4 cm at the waist.
And about 4 to 6 cm at the hip, or she cannot sit down. These are starting points, not laws. You confirm ease in the toile.

Most blocks are drafted as a quarter of the body, so you divide by four. For example, Ada drafts a fitted dress for a client with a 96 cm bust, and wants 6 cm of ease.
The body quarter is 96 divided by 4, which is 24 cm.
The ease per quarter is 6 divided by 4, which is 1.5 cm.
So the block quarter at the bust is 25.5 cm.
Check: 25.5 times 4 is 102 cm.
Blocks have no seam allowance. On the production pattern she adds 1.5 cm at the side seams. Seam allowance is sewn away, so it does not change the finished size.

The quarter method
Half the back, half the front
Each piece is one quarter of the body
Add a quarter of the ease to each
Formulas are starting points
The toile has the final word
With the quarter method, you draft half the back and half the front. Each is a quarter of the body width.
So each piece gets a quarter of the ease. For example, Kemi has a 96 cm bust and a 78 cm waist. With 6 cm of bust ease and 4 cm at the waist, that is 1.5 cm and 1 cm per quarter.
Every formula is a starting point.
Your toile, not the formula, has the final word.
Step by step
Drafting the back bodice
Centre back line; nape to waist 39 cm
Armhole depth: 96 / 8 + 10 = 22 cm
Bust line: 24 + 1.5 = 25.5 cm
Neck, shoulder 12.5 cm, armhole curve
Waist 20.5 cm: 2 cm at side, 3 cm dart
Draw the centre back line and mark the nape near the top. Measure down Kemi's nape to waist length, 39 cm, and square across for the waist.
Mark the armhole depth. A common starting value is bust divided by 8, plus 10 cm. For Kemi that is 22 cm. Square across. This is the bust line.
On the bust line, measure out a quarter of the bust plus ease. 24 plus 1.5 makes 25.5 cm. Square down for the side seam guide.
Draw the back neck curve and a sloping shoulder 12.5 cm long, then curve the armhole down to the side.
The waist quarter is 19.5 plus 1, which is 20.5 cm. The bust line is 25.5, so 5 cm must go. Take 2 cm at the side seam, and put 3 cm into a back waist dart.
The front is drafted the same way, with its bust point marked clearly.
Worked example
Finding the side bust dart
Back side seam: 39 minus 22 = 17 cm
Front side seam: 20.5 cm, longer for the bust
Difference: 3.5 cm side bust dart
Fold it closed: front now 17 cm too
Seams that sew together must be the same length.
Now compare the side seams. The back side seam is 39 minus 22, which is 17 cm.
The front side seam is 20.5 cm. It is longer, because the front waist dropped lower to go over the bust.
The side seams must be the same length to sew together. So the difference, 3.5 cm, becomes a side bust dart, pointing at the bust point and stopping 2.5 cm short of it.
Fold the dart closed and measure again. The front side seam is now 17 cm, matching the back.
Check your total too. 25.5 cm times 4 quarters is 102 cm, the body plus the ease.
Dart manipulation
Move the dart, keep the fit
Every front dart points at the bust point
Move it anywhere round the edge
Pivot, or slash and spread: same result
End it 2 to 3 cm short of the bust point
Both dart legs the same length
A dart is a wedge of fabric stitched away to shape flat cloth. On the front bodice, every dart points at the bust point.
So you can move it anywhere around the edge, shoulder, neckline or waist. The fit stays the same. Only the look changes.
Pivot the block on the bust point, or slash a paper copy and spread it. Both give the same result.
Stop bust darts 2 to 3 cm short of the bust point, or you get a sharp peak.
And keep both legs the same length, or the seam will not match.
For example, Halima in Kano moved a side dart to the shoulder, then turned it into a princess seam for an aso-ebi lace gown, with the same fit.

Quarter of the body plus quarter of the ease
Waist reduction: side seam plus a dart
Front minus back side seam = side bust dart
Darts move round the bust point
Correct the paper after every toile
To remember. Draft in quarters. The side seam difference becomes the bust dart. Move darts around the bust point. And never cut the real fabric until the toile fits.

Fabric first
Grain, shrinkage and print direction
Grain line arrow parallel to the selvedge
Shrinkage test on a 20 cm square
Brocade and directional prints: one way
Lay out every piece before you cut
The straight grain runs along the selvedge, the firm finished edge. Measure from both ends of each grain arrow to the selvedge. Both must be equal, or the garment can twist.
Do not guess shrinkage. Wash and dry a 20 cm square as the client will, then measure. If it is now 19 cm, it shrank 5 percent. Pre-wash, or add that to your lengths.
Brocade, damask and directional prints must be cut with every piece facing the same way.
And lay out all pieces before the scissors touch the fabric.
Heat safety
Pressing without damage
Cotton takes a hot iron. Many laces, sequins and synthetic linings melt at high heat.
Put plain cotton between the iron and delicate or shiny fabrics. Never press sequins.
Lift and lower the iron. Sliding it stretches fitted garments out of shape.
Always test the iron on a scrap first. Cotton takes a hot iron, but many laces, sequinned fabrics and synthetic linings melt or pucker at high heat.
Use a press cloth, a piece of plain cotton, between the iron and delicate or shiny fabric. Never press directly on sequins or metallic threads.
Press by lifting and lowering the iron, not sliding it, so fitted garments do not stretch. Press every seam as you sew.
Worked example
Will 6 yards be enough?
Bodice front and back: 45 cm
Two skirt panels: 2 x 125 = 250 cm
Sleeves: 35 cm; print matching: 30 cm
Shrinkage allowance: 15 cm
Total about 3.75 m of about 5.49 m
Tell the client how much fabric is left, before you cut.
For example, Amaka in Onitsha has 6 yards of ankara, about 5.49 m, for a flared gown and a headwrap. She lays her paper pieces on the folded width.
The bodice front and back sit side by side: 45 cm.
The skirt panels are too wide to sit side by side, so they go one after the other: 250 cm.
The sleeves take 35 cm. She adds 30 cm for matching the print.
Her shrinkage test showed 3 percent, so she adds 15 cm.
The total is about 3.75 m, leaving about 1.7 m for the headwrap.
She photographs the layout and tells the client before cutting, so there is no argument later about missing fabric.
Grading is not enlarging
Changes a lot
Bust: 4 cm per size
Waist: 4 cm per size
Hip: 4 cm per size
Changes a little
Neck: 1 cm per size
Shoulder: 0.3 cm per size
Nape to waist: 0.5 cm
Grading makes a pattern larger or smaller in a planned way. It is not photocopying it bigger. In real bodies, the bust, waist and hip change a lot between sizes. In this example chart, 4 cm each.
But the neck, shoulder and length change only a little. Enlarge everything by 10 percent and the dress gapes at the neckline. Build your own size chart from your real clients.
Step by step
Grading Kemi's bodice from L to XL
Bust 4 cm: each quarter grows 1 cm
Spread 0.5 cm, side seam out 0.5 cm
Length: spread 0.5 cm above the waist
Neck point out about 0.2 cm
Check: 26.5 x 4 = 106 cm
Grade only from a tested base block. Toile one graded size.
For example, Kemi's tested size L block is the base for 25 aso-ebi gowns. Six women measure close to XL.
The bust grows 4 cm. Divided by four quarters, that is 1 cm per quarter.
She cuts a vertical line from the armhole down to the waist and spreads it 0.5 cm, then moves the side seam out 0.5 cm. The waist grows the same way.
For length, she spreads a horizontal line between armhole and waist by 0.5 cm.
The neck grows only 1 cm, so the neck point moves out just about 0.2 cm.
Check it. The bust quarter is now 26.5 cm. Times 4 is 106 cm, the XL bust of 100 plus 6 cm of ease.
Then redraw the curves smoothly, label each size in a different colour, and test it.
Grace checks gown 14 of 20
Spec: bust 104, waist 86, hip 110 cm
Measured hip 108.5 cm: fails by 1.5 cm
2 cm seam allowance left: re-sew 0.4 cm out
Hip now 110.1 cm: within tolerance
A specification lists what the finished garment should measure. A tolerance is how far it may vary and still pass. For example, Grace in Port Harcourt allows 0.5 cm on girths and 1 cm on lengths.
Gown 14 should measure 104 cm at the bust, 86 at the waist and 110 at the hip.
She measures it flat. Bust and waist pass, but the hip is 108.5 cm. That is 1.5 cm small, so it fails.
There is 2 cm of seam allowance left, so she re-sews each side seam 0.4 cm closer to the edge at the hip.
The hip is now 110.1 cm. It passes, and the problem was found in her shop, not on the wedding morning.

Price your work, protect your orders, and show your skill.

Why this matters
A price covers four things
Materials you buy: lining, zips, thread
Labour: your hours, including pattern work
Overheads: rent, power, fuel, data
Profit, so the business can grow

Many skilled tailors earn less than they should, because they price by guessing. A good price covers four things. First, materials. Even when the client brings the lace, you buy lining, zips, thread and interfacing.
Second, your labour. Pattern work and fittings are skilled work, and belong in the price.
Third, overheads: rent, electricity, generator fuel and data, shared across the garments you finish each month.
And fourth, profit. If any one is missing, you are paying for the client's outfit yourself.
Worked example
Pricing a fitted lace gown
For example, Ifeoma in Lagos prices a fitted, lined lace gown. The client brings the lace.
Labour: 10 hours at 2,000
Overheads share
Naira prices are approximate.
Ifeoma in Lagos is pricing a fitted lace gown. All these figures are approximate.
Lining, zip, thread, interfacing and boning come to about 8,600 naira.
She wants 250,000 naira a month and sews about 125 hours a month. That is 2,000 naira an hour. The gown takes 10 hours, including pattern adjustment and two fittings. That is 20,000 naira.
Her monthly overheads are 130,000 naira, shared over about 40 garments. That is 3,250 naira per gown.
Her total cost is 31,850 naira. With 25 percent profit, she quotes about 40,000 naira.
She now knows that charging 25,000 would mean losing money on every gown.
Aso-ebi orders
One-off gown or group gown?
Pattern: 3 hours
Cut and sew: 6 hours
Labour about 20,000 naira
Aso-ebi, 20 gowns
Pattern shared: 0.4 hours each
Batch sewing: about 4.5 hours
Labour about 10,800 naira
A one-off gown takes about 10 hours of labour, including 3 hours of pattern work just for that client.

In an aso-ebi group of 20, one base pattern is graded and shared, and you cut and sew in batches. Labour drops to about 5.4 hours a gown. So you may offer a lower price, but only after calculating it.
Set a cut-off date for measurements and deposits, and refuse orders that would push you past the event.
Protect your money
Three rules that prevent disputes
For example half the price before cutting, and the balance before collection.
Confirm money in your bank, Opay or Moniepoint app. Never trust an SMS or screenshot.
Order form: style, fabric received, price, deposit, fitting and delivery dates.
Agree a deposit before you cut, for example half the price, with the balance before collection.
Fake bank transfer alerts are a known scam. Before you release a garment, check your own bank or wallet app, not an SMS or a screenshot from the customer.

And use a written order form. Most disputes come from things never written down: you said Friday, I wanted the neckline lower. Write the style, fabric received, price, deposit, fitting dates, delivery date and your alteration policy.
Planning backwards
Zainab plans back from the wedding
1 to 4 March: consult, measure, deposit
5 to 11 March: pattern and toile
12 March: first fitting
22 March: final fitting
26 March: delivery, three days early
Two fittings and a buffer, planned from the start.
For example, Zainab in Abuja gets an order on 1 March for a lace gown for a wedding on 29 March. She works backwards from the event.
From 1 to 4 March, consultation, measurements, deposit and the shrinkage test.
Pattern and toile from 5 to 11 March.
First fitting on 12 March, then sewing in lace.
Final fitting on 22 March.
Delivery on 26 March, three days before the wedding, so there is time for a last fix. She sends a WhatsApp reminder before each fitting.
Your portfolio
Photos that sell your skill
Daylight by a window, or outside in shade
Plain wall or cloth as background
Front, side and back views
Close-ups: matched print, zip, inside finish
Ask permission before you post
Your portfolio sells your skill when you are not in the room. A phone is enough. Shoot in daylight, not harsh midday sun.
Use a plain background.
Take front, side and back views.
Then close-ups of what clients pay for: matched print at the seams, a neat invisible zip, the inside finishing.
Always get the client's permission before posting photos of her, and never post her measurements, address or phone number. Use a dress form if she prefers.
Key points
Remember
Materials, labour, overheads and profit
Hourly rate = income needed / hours sewn
Calculate before discounting group orders
Deposit first; confirm payment in your app
Plan back from the event with a buffer

To remember. Price from real costs, with profit on top, not instead of your labour. Calculate before you discount. Take a deposit and confirm every payment yourself. And plan fittings back from the event.
